The school shark, Galeorhinus galeus, is a large, long-lived carcharhiniform found in temperate continental shelf waters worldwide. At the time of parturition, neonates typically emerge at a total length of around 32 cm [Lb = around 32 cm], though recorded values for this length at birth range from 30 to 36 cm. The corresponding wet weight at birth is approximately 140 grams [Wwb = approximately 140 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves these young sharks rely upon before commencing independent foraging. Gestation is completed after an estimated gestation period of 12 months, a duration that scales predictably with maternal body size in this family. Following the completion of the gestation period, pups are born in shallow nursery grounds during late spring and summer, where they benefit from warm, food-rich conditions that support rapid early growth. The reliance on such productive coastal habitats is a key life-history strategy, reducing early mortality risks for these immature individuals before they recruit into the offshore adult population.

Sexual maturation in female school sharks is a comparatively protracted process, with puberty occurring at approximately 17 years after birth [tp = approximately 17 years after birth], a remarkably late age that is characteristic of many slow-growing at a temperature of 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C] elasmobranchs. At the onset of sexual maturity, females typically measure about 155 cm [Lp = about 155 cm] in length and carry a wet weight at puberty of roughly 16,400 grams [Wwp = roughly 16,400 grams]. Males, by contrast, reach sexual maturity earlier, typically at around 12 years since birth [tp = around 12 years since birth] at a temperature of 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C]. The total length at puberty for males is 121 cm [Lp = 121 cm], and they achieve a corresponding weight at puberty of approximately 7,760 grams [Wwp = approximately 7,760 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in size and maturation timing is common in many carcharhinid sharks and is often interpreted as a consequence of differing reproductive investments between the sexes.

Adult school sharks display striking sexual dimorphism in ultimate size, with females reaching a substantially larger asymptotic body length than males. The ultimate total length for females is recorded at 199 cm [Li = 199 cm], a size that supports their greater capacity for litter production. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 34,900 grams [Wwi = approximately 34,900 grams]. Males, in contrast, attain a smaller ultimate total length of 178 cm [Li = 178 cm], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of around 24,900 grams [Wwi = around 24,900 grams]. This female-biased size dimorphism is a common trait among large, long-lived elasmobranchs and is believed to be energetically favorable for accommodating developing litters, as the spacious body cavity can hold a greater number of pups and larger yolk stores.

Under the thermal conditions typical of temperate coastal waters, which average 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C], the reproductive schedule of school sharks is characterized by a low annual output. Females are thought to produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with the number of pups per litter ranging from 6 to 52 pups [N_R_i = per litter ranging from 6 to 52 pups] depending on maternal size and condition. This relatively low reproductive frequency is a classic characteristic of a K-selected species, trading high fecundity for larger offspring size and extended parental investment in the form of yolk provisioning. The lifespan of this species is also notable, with the maximum longevity recorded at approximately 55 years [am = approximately 55 years] at a temperature of 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C]. Some studies report a slightly narrower range, from 46 to 59 years, placing the school shark among the longest-lived coastal carcharhinids.

The early life stages of the school shark are particularly vulnerable, and the timing of key developmental events is tightly linked to the ambient temperature of the oceanic environment. The age at birth, from the moment of zygote formation, is calculated to be approximately 366 days [ab = approximately 366 days] at a water temperature of 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C]. This long prenatal period is followed by a slow juvenile growth phase, meaning that both female and male sharks experience a long delay before they can participate in reproduction for the first time. For perspective, in a stable environment maintained at 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C], a female shark would not begin producing her own offspring until she is 17 years [tp = 17 years] of age, underscoring the high generation time and extreme demographic sensitivity of this species to any increase in fishing mortality.
